To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) pigeons do not prefer reinforcement after a delay to reinforcement on a fixed-intervals schedule, (b) when they do show a preference, it is not for reinforcement after a delay per se, but rather for the light off that is present during the delay, (c) when pigeons show a preference, the preference is smaller than when the two intervals are different, and (d) the small preferences are caused by the light off.

(1) when the time between a key peck and the delivery of reinforcement was equated, pigeoms did not respond differently to delayed and fixed-interval reinforcement, (2) the small preference sometimes shown for the fixed-interval schedule was caused by the absence during the delay of light, and (3) these results are consistent with the notion that the probability of a response is controlled by the time between that response and reinforcement, regardless of whether other responses intervene.
pigeons show little or no preference for reinforcement after a delay versus reinforcement after a temporally equated fixed interval.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of the time between a behavioral event and reinforcement.
the effect of a delay of reinforcement upon the probability of a response.
the effects of delayed reinforcers on the behavior that precedes their delivery.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, in the absence of any other information, the time between a behavior and its reinforcement controls the probability that that behavior will occur.
the delay-of-reinforcement effect is not a separate phenomenon, but is merely a special case of the fixed-interval schedule of reinforcement.
the effects of a delay on prior responding are due to the temporal separation of the response and its consequence.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
delay of reinforcement has effects on prior responding which are similar in magnitude and form to those produced by the time between response and reinforcement.
the effects of delay are not due to a delay of reinforcement but to the temporal properties of the interval between response and reinforcement.
the effects of a delay on prior responding are due to the delay itself, and not to the fact that it is a delay.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the effects of delay are due to the delay itself and not the absence of reinforcement during the delay.
, in the case of fixed-interval responding, it is not the time since the last reinforcer, but the time since the most recent response that is the critical determinant of the response rate.

the effects of delay and fixed-interval schedules on responding can be equated by making interreinforcement time equal, but that the fixed-interval schedule is more efficient at generating the effects of delay.
